rv.q: But we don’t care enough about the chase they give us.
The show has a slick, polished surface that conceals a surprising amount of heart, and while it's not a masterpiece, it's definitely a crowd-pleaser that knows how to entertain.
That musical sound and the perfs from Butz and Tveit (with assists from the briefly-seen Butler and Hart) offer considerable entertainment value.
Sadly, though, this “Catch” of the day is not especially compelling.
Yet “Catch Me If You Can” flounders.

Director Jack O'Brien, writer Terrence McNally, composer Marc Shaiman and co-lyricist Scott Wittman have made a slick, professional, conscientious and uninspired show that strains to fit Frank Abagnale Jr.'s improbably true tale into a stylized box of sentimentality and ho-hum retro-routines.
Or roused or touched or more than mildly entertained, for about 90 percent of the time.
Broadway's winning new Catch Me if You Can gives you lots of reasons to love the musical.
What should have been a fun lark of a story seems almost stodgy, like your grandmother's idea of a good time.
Still, in failing to deliver a youthful protagonist you can really cheer for, this Catch Me If You Can may leave you feeling a bit cheated.
Under Jack O'Brien's impersonal direction, the talented cast works hard to make an impression.
"Catch Me If You Can" aims for the clouds but only occasionally gets there.
The variety show gimmick, which on paper might seem cute, seems to suck the life out of the show, despite the fact there is much to like here, even outstanding about CATCH ME IF YOU CAN.
Frank slipped off into the night, and I don't feel as if I found him.
That's the feeling you get watching "Catch Me If You Can," a shiny and well-acted, but ineffectual, musical that, for most of the evening, goes every which way but forward.
But in spite of so much promise, "Catch Me If You Can" is so disappointing that it will leave you wishing you could travel back in time and watch "Hairspray" again.
There's so much that works about Catch Me if You Can that it's easy to overlook what doesn't.
“Catch Me If You Can” expertly provides a darned good story, a perky score, tip-top performances and glossy visuals.

New Broadway shows this spring are lousy with cads. There’s J. Pierrepont Finch in "How to Succeed in Business Without Really Trying," Harry Brock in "Born Yesterday" and pretty much all the dudes in "That Championship Season." With the hero of "Catch Me If You Can," add one more scoundrel.

cn.t: Critics find this slick, well-crafted musical disappointingly earthbound despite strong performances from Norbert Leo Butz and a tuneful '60s score—it's professionally executed but struggles to soar until nearly the end.
